Lots of debate about Goldman Sach's 2027 oil view (surplus; bearish) published earlier today. But let me flag one item that's not yet getting enough attention:

"... We estimate that China's total oil demand peaked in 2025..."

MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: With data for the first 10 days of November, we can see two trends emerging on Persian Gulf oil exports (ex Iran): 

A) After a very strong start of the month, crude oil flows are now materially lower, running about ~2.0m b/d below than full-month October (equal to 85% of pre-war levels, from 100% in October). The drop is widespread, but particularly acute for Kuwaiti flows. 

B) At the same time, exports of petroleum refined products are significantly higher than in Sep and Oct, suggesting a deliberate effort to prioritize them at the expense of crude. Kuwait and UAE are mostly behind the boost of refined products. All said, Nov 1-10 refined petroleum products exports are running at ~65% of prewar levels, up from 50%-40% in Oct-Sep.

But all together, and ex-Iran Middle East total oil flows are lower than Oct, but roughly on par with September. The composition has changed, however, with crude materially lower, and refined products materially higher.

BREAKING: For the first time in >2 months, US average diesel retail prices have fallen below $6 a gallon. 

At a nationwide average of $5.9989 a gallon, diesel is down now ~8% from its peak in late September, but remains nearly 60% more expensive than a year ago.

U.S. GAS STOCKS have continued to climb slightly faster and longer into the start of the heating season than normal. Inventories were 101 billion cubic feet (+3% or +0.45 standard deviations) above the prior ten-year seasonal average on November 6 and the surplus had doubled from 51 bcf (+1% or +0.20σ) on October 1. Excess stocks have kept front-month futures prices below the fuel-switching threshold with coal to encourage maximum use of gas by generators:
And… someone forgot to tell oil prices.

COT on #forex – dollar longs cut despite broad USD strength

The latest IMM positioning data, covering the post-US midterm election week to 10 November, shows an 18% reduction in the aggregate dollar net long against eight major currency futures to USD 29.6 billion, despite broad dollar strength during the reporting period which drove the BBG DXY to an 18-month high. 

Speculative dollar selling was led by short covering in EUR and GBP, alongside renewed buying of JPY. The euro net short fell by 21k contracts to 136k, while the yen net long rose by 21k to 123k contracts, hitting a one-year high.

The Australian dollar was the major exception, with speculators adding another 22.3k contracts to an already substantial bearish position, lifting the net short to a fresh record of 152k contracts, equivalent to USD 10.4 billion. The Canadian dollar also remained under pressure, with its net short expanding by 9.2k contracts to 32.6k.

The broader message: Despite the dollar's underlying strength, speculative positioning was cut as oil prices eased after the election, before the subsequent hotter-than-expected US CPI print reinforced expectations of further Fed tightening.

COT on #commodities – another week of aggressive long liquidation

The latest COT report, covering the week to 10 November, captures the aftermath of the US midterm elections but precedes last week's hotter-than-expected US CPI print and renewed concerns about further Fed tightening.

Speculators continued to head for the exits, with broad-based selling across energy and agriculture driving a 35% slump in the combined net long across 25 major commodity futures contracts to 507k lots.

Energy: The combined Brent and WTI net long slumped by another 66k contracts to a four-month low of just 202k, as traders increasingly positioned for a potential supply surplus amid recovering Middle East production.

Agriculture: The dramatic unwinding of bullish grain and soybean bets continued. Having reached a record net long above one million contracts just seven weeks ago, the combined position has now collapsed back towards neutral. Soybeans and soybean products suffered particularly heavy selling, while fresh short positions continued to build in corn and wheat.

Precious metals: Gold was the notable exception, attracting a 10% increase in the net long to 114k contracts, mostly due to fresh longs. Unfortunately for the bulls, the subsequent inflation surprise and renewed dollar and yield strength made that a poorly timed move. Silver and platinum positioning remained subdued, while palladium shorts continued to rise.

The broader message: Speculative appetite for commodities continues to deteriorate, with long liquidation rather than aggressive fresh short selling driving much of the decline. While this reflects growing macroeconomic and supply concerns, the ongoing reduction in speculative length may eventually help lay the groundwork for the next rebound, potentially not until early next year.

#Commodities:
#CrudeOil: Brent rebounds to USD 96.6 after touching a low of USD 94.32 earlier today, supported by reports of Iranian drone attacks on a US base in Bahrain and tankers striking mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, the IEA estimates that global oil supply will exceed demand by around 2 million barrels per day this quarter, driven by a strong recovery in output from Persian Gulf exporters. Increased crude oil supply, however, does little to ease tightness in distillate fuels and LNG, where prices remain elevated amid a slow recovery in Middle Eastern refining capacity, production and shipments.

Metals: #Gold extends its decline towards USD 3,840 after last week's technical breakdown saw prices close at a 13-month low. Persistent inflation continues to fuel expectations of further US rate hikes, while concerns over the AI sector weigh on broader risk sentiment. #Silver leads the sell-off, dropping 3% to USD 47.3 and lifting the gold-silver ratio to a one-year high above 81. Meanwhile, #copper has slumped to a four-month low of USD 6.11 per pound, driven by speculative long liquidation as an otherwise constructive supply/demand outlook is challenged by the technology-sector rout and broad-based weakness in China's October economic data.
